bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo

bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds

bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.

Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.

bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.

bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

bivy.name: Crescent Lake
bivy.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about three hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
bivy.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

bivy.name: Merritt Lake
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
bivy.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

bivy.name: Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight
bivy.notes: The lookout itself: you may walk to it and, if it is staffed and the lookout is willing, speak to whoever is on duty, but you may not stay in it or expect shelter from it. Plan the day accordingly and do not treat the building as a bail-out option in bad weather. The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.
bivy.water: None at all, and none for the last several miles of trail in either direction. There is one seasonal spring close to the Round Mountain trailhead that runs early in the year and cannot be relied on; past it the trail is dry the whole way. From the west, the last water is Merritt Lake, about three miles back. Carry everything.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is required at the Round Mountain trailhead. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery — none of Nason Ridge is designated wilderness. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the surrounding forest is dry enough that fire restrictions are near-permanent through the summer, which is rather the point of the building on the summit.
bivy.capacity: None for the public. This is an active Forest Service fire lookout, staffed through the summer fire season, and it is NOT available to sleep in, not rentable, and not one of the lookouts in this state that take overnight visitors. Treat it as a staffed workplace: the summit is a fine place to stand, and the building is somebody's post. There is no established campsite at the lookout either, and the ground around it is narrow open ridge crest.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

bivy.name: Merritt Lake
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
bivy.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

bivy.name: Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight
bivy.notes: The lookout itself: you may walk to it and, if it is staffed and the lookout is willing, speak to whoever is on duty, but you may not stay in it or expect shelter from it. Plan the day accordingly and do not treat the building as a bail-out option in bad weather. The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.
bivy.water: None at all, and none for the last several miles of trail in either direction. There is one seasonal spring close to the Round Mountain trailhead that runs early in the year and cannot be relied on; past it the trail is dry the whole way. From the west, the last water is Merritt Lake, about three miles back. Carry everything.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is required at the Round Mountain trailhead. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery — none of Nason Ridge is designated wilderness. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the surrounding forest is dry enough that fire restrictions are near-permanent through the summer, which is rather the point of the building on the summit.
bivy.capacity: None for the public. This is an active Forest Service fire lookout, staffed through the summer fire season, and it is NOT available to sleep in, not rentable, and not one of the lookouts in this state that take overnight visitors. Treat it as a staffed workplace: the summit is a fine place to stand, and the building is somebody's post. There is no established campsite at the lookout either, and the ground around it is narrow open ridge crest.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Basin Creek Camp
bivy.notes: The closest designated camp to the Horseshoe Basin trail junction, which sits at about 3,600 ft on the valley trail, so it is the practical base for anything up in the cirque. It has a separate cooking area, a bear box and its own privy. Capacity is tiny — three sites — so a party of four fills most of it and a weekend permit is not something to count on. From here the basin trail climbs roughly 1,300 ft in about 1.5 miles to the Black Warrior Mine and the waterfall headwall below Ripsaw Ridge and Buckner's north side.
bivy.water: Reliable — Basin Creek runs beside the camp all season
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA); designated camp reserved by site on Recreation.gov, with roughly 40% of inventory held for walk-up the day before at Marblemount or Golden West in Stehekin. Per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: 3 sites, 12 people total

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway to the basin, at the end of what used to be the upper Stehekin Valley road. It has a privy, fire rings, picnic table and bear boxes, though the boxes are set well back from the cooking area. ACCESS IS THE THING TO PLAN AROUND: the road washed out for the last time in 2003 and the Stehekin shuttle now turns around at High Bridge, so reaching Cottonwood from the boat means an extra day of walking the old roadbed rather than the bus ride older descriptions assume. Check the current shuttle schedule before committing — upper-valley service has varied year to year.
bivy.water: Reliable — creek water a short walk below the camp
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp, same Recreation.gov reservation and walk-up system as the rest of the complex.
bivy.capacity: Several sites, including one that takes a larger group and a few small secluded ones

bivy.name: Pelton Basin Camp
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: A set of hand-built rock-walled tent platforms at the toe of the glacier, at the top of Sahale Arm. It is high, exposed and above the last dependable water, so late-season parties should plan to melt snow or carry up from lower on the arm. For the Horseshoe Basin peaks it is a high camp rather than a basin camp — it serves approaches that cross Sahale Arm and drop toward Doubtful Lake and the head of the basin, and it puts you on the right side of the divide for Buckner's north aspect. Reported elevation varies slightly between sources.
bivy.water: Unreliable — snowmelt and glacier runoff only, and the seasonal trickles commonly dry up by late summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; one of the most contested designated camps in the park. Realistically needs the early-access lottery or the general on-sale window in late April.
bivy.capacity: 4 sites, 4 people per site

bivy.name: Doubtful Lake Camp
bivy.notes: Doubtful Lake lies in a cirque below Sahale Arm, reached by a spur that drops off the arm trail. It is the natural middle camp on the Sahale Arm variation of the approach, breaking up a long crossing between Cascade Pass and the head of Horseshoe Basin. Water is the one thing never in question here, which matters if the alternative is Sahale Glacier Camp late in the season. The spur loses meaningful elevation off the arm, so factor the reclimb into the next day.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus its inlet and outlet streams
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camping at the lake, reserved or walked up like the other Cascade Pass-area sites.
bivy.capacity: A small designated camp at the lake, site count not published. Treat it as a handful of spots rather than a place a large party can count on.

bivy.name: Buckner cross-country zone bivy
bivy.notes: The option for climbers who want to sleep on the route rather than at a valley camp — high bivies on moraine, slab or snow under Buckner's north side and the Ripsaw Ridge peaks. Zone rules are strict and worth reading before you go: camp at least a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight, and only on snow, rock or bare ground. No meadow camping, nothing within 100 ft of water, no fires. Because the permit is walk-up only, a trip built around a zone bivy is one you cannot lock in ahead of time — carry a fallback.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent — snowmelt and seasonal streams in the upper basin, dependable early, thin or gone by late season
bivy.permit: NPS cross-country zone permit required, WALK-UP ONLY. Buckner is not among the zones that take advance reservations, so it cannot be booked on Recreation.gov and must be picked up in person, generally no more than a day ahead.
bivy.capacity: 6 people per party, 6 parties per night in the zone

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
bivy.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.
bivy.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat gravel and snow platforms along the moraine crest; the busiest camp on the north side and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
bivy.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.
bivy.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
bivy.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback

bivy.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
bivy.notes: Pushing camp onto the glacier below the Black Buttes cuts a real chunk out of summit day and puts you above most of the weather that sits on the moraine. It costs you a fully exposed camp on snow, so platforms need walls, and everything about the site depends on that year's crevasse pattern — what was a flat bench one August can be broken up the next. Parties are already roped and on glacier travel terrain to reach it, which rules it out for anyone wanting a simple carry. Wind is the usual reason people retreat from here to the Hogsback.
bivy.water: None you can rely on — this is a melt-snow camp, so budget fuel accordingly. Occasional surface runoff appears on the rock of the Black Buttes in hot spells but should not be planned around.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

bivy.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
bivy.notes: The saddle between Colfax Peak and the main summit is occasionally used as a very high bivy by strong parties shortening summit day, and more often as an emergency stop by parties caught out by weather or a slow descent. It is fully exposed to wind and to whatever the mountain is doing, with no shelter of any kind, and the Roman Wall above it is not somewhere to be improvising in a storm. Treat it as a contingency rather than a plan unless the forecast is settled and your party is fast. It is also the last place on the route with any option other than continuing up or going down.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry everything from lower on the route.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties at most; an exposed high point rather than a campsite

bivy.name: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
bivy.notes: The standard Easton Glacier high camp, reached by following the Railroad Grade moraine up from Schriebers Meadow and Morovitz Meadow. The basin gives real wind protection, which is why it is preferred over the more scenic but more exposed ground on the moraine crest itself. The gravel road in is snowbound into June in most years and is rough enough to be worth checking before a long drive. There have been seasons with no toilet facilities anywhere on the mountain, with blue bags issued free at the Sedro-Woolley ranger office, so carry a pack-out system.
bivy.water: Contested and season-dependent. Some parties find runoff at the north end of the camp and on the rocky ground above it; others arrive to find nothing exposed at all and must melt snow. Plan for melting and treat running water as a bonus.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — the approach runs through the Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and the upper moraine into Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit. A recreation pass is required to park at the Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead. Registering your climb at a ranger station is voluntary but sensible.
bivy.capacity: The main climbers' camp on the south side, in a sheltered sandy basin at the crest of the moraine; multiple tent sites, busy in July and August

bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
bivy.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback

bivy.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes

bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

bivy.name: Silver Springs Campground
bivy.notes: The practical roadhead base for a Little Tahoma trip, on the White River about a mile outside the park's White River entrance and a short drive from the Fryingpan Creek trailhead. Its usefulness is timing: the park's own drive-in campground on this side is the highest in the park and normally the last to open, typically not until late June, so for an early-season attempt on Little Tahoma this is often the nearest bed available. It is low, forested and comfortable, with real water and real toilets, and worth nothing at all for acclimatisation. Book it if you want an unhurried night before the approach without spending a wilderness permit on it.
bivy.water: Drinking water on site during the operating season, with flush and vault toilets. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed Forest Service campground outside the park boundary, reservable through the federal booking system. It sits outside the national park, which means it is not subject to the park entrance fee or to any timed-entry reservation the park may be operating for its corridors; you pay and queue for those the following morning on the way in. This covers the campground only, and has nothing to do with either the wilderness permit or the climbing fee, both of which you still need.
bivy.capacity: Around 55 individual drive-in sites plus one group site taking roughly 20 to 50 people; tents and RVs, no hookups

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

bivy.name: Slide Lake
bivy.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
bivy.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.

bivy.name: Jug Lake
bivy.notes: THE BASE FOR MOUNT CHAVAL, which sits immediately southwest of Snowking and has three standard approaches and one longer non-standard one, none of them simple and all of them brushy. This is the most used of them. Park at the prominent switchback where Arrow Creek meets Illabot Creek Road at about 2,220 feet, roughly 16 miles up the road, and follow an old overgrown fishermen's path up the right bank of Arrow Creek to the lake; it is reasonably defined and flagged at the doubtful places. From the camps on the north shore the route climbs north-northeast to gain the ridge around 5,200 feet, traverses to the pass between the two points just over 6,350 feet, and then commits to a genuine cross-country bushwhack through cliffy ground into the Arrow Creek amphitheatre before steep hillsides and talus lead to the mountain. Reckon on about ten miles and 4,600 feet for the round trip from the road, and on the vegetation being the crux. No elevation is recorded for the lake because no confident figure was found.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable. Nothing dependable above it once you are on the ridge and in the Arrow Creek amphitheatre.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Parking is at the Arrow Creek switchback on Illabot Creek Road rather than at a developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass may not apply there in the way it does at Slide Lake; check with the district rather than assume either way. No fires at the lake, and pack out human waste.
bivy.capacity: Several good camps on the north side of the lake, roomy by the standards of this zone. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Gunn Basin, below Tailgunner Pass
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Tailgunner, and it turns a very long day into a comfortable one. The climbers' path leaves the Barclay Creek road below the Barclay Lake trailhead, crosses the creek, and then climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest on a faint boot track, with dirt-covered slabs, a narrow traverse under cliffs and an exposed crossing above a waterfall before the angle relents into the basin. Reckon on three to four hours to camp with overnight loads. From here Tailgunner itself is an easy hour of slabby scrambling, and Gunn Peak and Wing Peak are both within reach the same morning, which is the usual reason parties carry a camp up at all. The shoulder of Tailgunner holds a shallow tarn perched right on the lip of the drop, and it is the obvious place to put a tent, but it is exposed and there is nothing between it and the weather. Season is roughly July to early October; earlier than that the traverse under the cliffs holds hard snow and the waterfall crossing is genuinely dangerous. The approach path is not maintained, is easy to lose on the descent, and should be tracked on the way up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns in the basin through midsummer, and a small stream draining the pass. Both can dry to nothing by late August in a thin year — carry the day's water up from Barclay Creek if the season has been hot.
bivy.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit or quota for camping. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at the Barclay Lake trailhead and at the pullouts either side of it. Stoves rather than fires — the basin is at the edge of timberline and the scattered wood there is what holds the heather together.
bivy.capacity: Open heather benches and slabs holding perhaps three or four small tents, scattered rather than clustered. No constructed sites, no toilet, no fire ring worth using.

bivy.name: Barclay Creek roadhead pullouts
bivy.notes: This is a staging camp rather than a destination, and it exists because the Tailgunner and Gunn climbers' path leaves the road here rather than at the lake. Sleeping at the roadhead lets a party start the steep forest climb in the dark and reach the basin before the day heats up, which matters on a south-facing approach. The spur road with the clearing drops off the main road a short distance below the pit toilet at the Barclay Lake trailhead; the path itself heads right before that clearing and is unsigned. Do not confuse this with Barclay Lake, which is a maintained walk-in with established lakeside sites and is covered elsewhere. The road is plowed nowhere and is gated by snow from roughly late November to April, which puts the winter ascent of Tailgunner well out of reach for most parties. Expect log trucks and weekend traffic through the summer, and expect the trailhead lot to be full by mid-morning on any fine Saturday.
bivy.water: Barclay Creek runs beside the road and is the only supply. Treat it.
bivy.permit: National forest, dispersed camping, no permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead parking itself. Campfire restrictions follow the district and are common from July onward — check before assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.capacity: A handful of rough dispersed pullouts and one small clearing on a spur road a short walk below the trailhead. Room for two or three vehicles to sleep beside, not a campground.

bivy.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
bivy.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its availability as a question to answer before you drive rather than an assumption. When the road is cut at the North Fork bridge it is unreachable from the Beckler River side entirely. Even when it is open it is a low, damp, mosquito-heavy site in early summer, and its value is convenience rather than pleasure — it puts a party within twenty minutes of the start of the Spire approach, which is worth a great deal on a climb that wants a pre-dawn departure. Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground serve the same road system and are covered in the neighbouring zone, so check those first if this one is closed.
bivy.water: River water only, treated. There is no potable supply.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee when it is operating. No wilderness permit is involved at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A small forest campground of a dozen or so sites in second-growth beside the North Fork Skykomish, with vault toilets and no water system.
